subject: Biology
title: Smallpox: The First Vaccine
description: A micro-lesson that makes Smallpox: The First Vaccine usable.

hook.text: In 1796, Edward Jenner injected a boy with cowpox pus—and proved it protected against deadly smallpox.

buildup.text: Milkmaids who caught cowpox—a mild disease—seemed immune to smallpox. Jenner tested the idea.

discovery.text: Cowpox virus was similar enough to smallpox that the immune system recognized both.

twist.text: It took nearly 200 years, but in 1980, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated—the only human disease eliminated.

climax.text: Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone before eradication.

punchline.text: A milkmaid's immunity saved the world.

quiz.question: What animal disease did Jenner use to create the first vaccine?

details.summary: In 1796, Edward Jenner demonstrated that inoculation with cowpox virus protected against deadly smallpox, creating the world's first vaccine. This discovery launched the field of immunology and led to the complete eradication of smallpox in 1980, the greatest public health achievement.

takeaways: Jenner's cowpox inoculation in 1796 created the first vaccine
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 through global vaccination
Cross-reactive immunity between related viruses was Jenner's key insight

faq.question: How did Jenner know cowpox would protect against smallpox?
faq.answer: Jenner observed that milkmaids who caught cowpox from cows never got smallpox. He tested this by inoculating a boy with cowpox material, then deliberately exposing him to smallpox. The boy did not develop smallpox, proving cross-protective immunity between the related viruses.

faq.question: Could smallpox ever come back?
faq.answer: Samples of smallpox virus are stored in two secure laboratories in the US and Russia. Routine vaccination stopped decades ago, leaving most of the world unprotected. While natural return is impossible since it was eradicated, biosecurity concerns keep preparedness plans active.
